tier_reason: First-party README benchmark blocks (AVX, SSE, word-wise and byte-wise runs of BenchmarkBytes; benchmark code is public in xor_test.go) with no CPU model, Go version or flags, so tier C. The SSE row was measured on assembly that was rewritten later the same day to fix a segfault, which also caps it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README BenchmarkBytes table (committed 2018-07-06 in 000cb37; unknown AVX2-capable CPU, GOMAXPROCS 4, Go version unstated): AVX 65k 67217.99 MB/s vs byte-wise loop 1684.45 MB/s (39.9x, derived from page data) and word-wise loop 13203.25 MB/s (5.09x, derived); 1024 B AVX 66089.39 vs byte-wise 1677.18 (39.4x, derived) and word-wise 11455.33 MB/s (5.77x, derived); 16 B AVX 2579.65 vs byte-wise 1263.77 (2.04x, derived) and word-wise 2170.17 MB/s (1.19x, derived); SSE 65k 32619.21 MB/s (2.47x over word-wise, derived). README conclusion: '2-40 times faster than a naive for loop'. The Block row (13546.30 MB/s for 16 bytes, committed 2018-10-11) is the library's own word-wise Go function compared with its Bytes/16 (2579.65 MB/s, 5.25x derived; README says 'about 6 times'), not a baseline comparison.
corrections.hardware: not stated (the AVX2 path ran, so an AVX2-capable x86-64 CPU; GOMAXPROCS 4 from the -4 suffix)
corrections.workload: xor of byte slices of 16 B, 1024 B and 65536 B, run in place on one zeroed buffer (Bytes(buf, buf, buf)) with SetBytes counting one stream; plus a specialised 16-byte Block function
corrections.caveats: No CPU model, Go version or flags; GOMAXPROCS 4 is the only setup detail. The README's AVX/SSE/word-wise/byte-wise numbers were committed on 2018-07-06 (000cb37). The SSE row predates commit 62a404d ('fix SSE segfault', same day), which rewrote the SSE loops: the measured code XORed from memory operands that fault on unaligned input (the benchmark's buffers happened to be aligned). The AVX path was dispatched on cpu.X86.HasAVX while using 256-bit integer VPXOR, which needs AVX2. It crashed with an illegal instruction on AVX-only CPUs such as the i7-3770 (issue #2) until PR #3 on 2021-03-22. That bug did not affect the measured path. The 40x headline is against a byte-wise loop that, in 2018, still had per-iteration bounds checks (BCE hints were added in 43ff724, 2020). Against the word-wise loop the gain is 1.2-5.8x. The benchmark aliases dst, a and b to one zeroed buffer, so the working set is a third of a real three-buffer xor. The modern Go incumbent, crypto/subtle.XORBytes (exported in Go 1.20; its amd64 assembly is a 16-byte SSE2 loop), was not benchmarked. fastxor's own SSE row is the closer analogue, so the AVX2 gain over today's stdlib is plausibly about 2x, not 5-40x (inference, not measured). There is no VZEROUPPER after the AVX2 loop. The author calls it a first try at Go assembly. amd64 only; other architectures use plain Go loops. 12 commits, last change 2021-03-22.

notes: README numbers match the record; the ratios are derived from page data. Main shortcomings: no hardware or Go version; the 40x figure is against a bounds-checked byte loop (5x against word-wise); the SSE row was measured on code later fixed for a segfault; and Go's crypto/subtle.XORBytes (SSE2 asm) was never compared. Not a duplicate of any catalog entry.

tier_reason: First-party README tables comparing BenchmarkTest with BenchmarkGoTest (code public in test_test.go, same sizes and memset setup), with the README's own speedup column. No CPU model, Go version or flags are given, so tier C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README speedup table (committed 2017-02-23 in 2eb5216; unknown CPU, GOMAXPROCS 8, Go version unstated), naive Go byte loop to go-byte-test: 32 B 893.80 to 4488.67 MB/s (5.02x), 128 B 15.45x, 1K 1177.11 to 40050.28 MB/s (34.02x), 16K 42.28x, 128K 36.34x, 1M 24.66x, 16M 14.67x, 128M 14.71x, 512M 1172.27 to 17316.31 MB/s (14.77x).
corrections.caveats: No CPU model, Go version or flags; only GOMAXPROCS 8 can be read from the -8 suffix. The README table was committed on 2017-02-23. The assembly was touched on 2018-04-22 only to replace hand-encoded PTEST bytes with the mnemonic (48837c9) and to drop the tmthrgd/asm generator; neither is a correctness fix. The baseline is a naive byte-at-a-time range loop written inline in the benchmark. A uint64-wise Go loop, or a stdlib SIMD route such as bytes.Count(data, []byte{value}) == len(data) through internal/bytealg, was not compared and would narrow the gap. The 34-42x peaks are at L1/L2-resident sizes; from 16M up it is memory-bound at about 17 GB/s (14.7x). The benchmark data is all equal to the value, so it measures the full-scan case only. The assembly uses PSHUFB (SSSE3) and PINSRB/PTEST (SSE4.1) with no CPUID check: amd64 CPUs without SSE4.1 (pre-Penryn Intel, AMD K10) will fault. It also uses R15, which Go's assembler reserves under -dynlink. amd64 only; other targets get the plain Go loop. Repository archived, 1 star, 12 commits.

notes: README numbers match the record exactly (16M is 14.67x, 128K 36.34x, both added). Main shortcomings: no hardware or Go version; a naive byte-loop baseline only; no runtime SSE4.1 check; archived and practically unused (1 star). Not a duplicate; go-memset and go-hex are separate tmthrgd entries.

corrections.caveats: CPU model, Go version and flags are not stated. The README numbers were refreshed on 2018-01-11, alongside the switch of the Go path to math/bits and of Travis to go1.9. The later 2018 assembly commits are formatting and generator removal, not correctness fixes. The baseline already uses the POPCNT-backed math/bits.OnesCount64 intrinsic over an unsafe []uint64 view. The 1.5-2.9x gain comes from 4x unrolling into separate destination registers, which the asm comments say is meant to dodge Intel's POPCNT false output dependency, an erratum of older Intel cores. Gc's per-call POPCNT feature check also costs the baseline time (removable with GOAMD64=v2 on Go 1.18+); this is an inference, not measured. So the gap is likely smaller on newer CPUs and compilers. At 512 MiB both sides are memory-bound (1.5x). For []uint64 input of 32 B the gain is only 1.2x. The package is derived in part from Hideaki Ohno's MIT-licensed go-popcount (Count64, hasPOPCNT, tests), though it is not a GitHub fork. amd64 only, with a CPUID check for POPCNT; other targets use the Go loop. Repository archived.

notes: README numbers match the record; the ratios are derived from page data, and the CountSlice64 rows were added. The licence is BSD-3-Clause plus MIT portions (both OSI, so copyable stands). Main shortcomings: no CPU model or Go version; a modest 1.5-2.9x gain over the math/bits intrinsic loop that likely shrinks on CPUs without the POPCNT false-dependency erratum; archived. Not a duplicate of any catalog entry (libpopcnt and sse-popcount are separate C/C++ entries).
